To ostracize someone means to deliberately exclude a person from a group and treat them as if they no longer belong — cutting them off from social interaction, acceptance, and belonging.

When a person is ostracized, the group doesn't just ignore them casually. They make a conscious, collective decision to push that person out of their circle. The person is still physically present — they haven't moved away — but everyone around them acts as though they are invisible, unwelcome, or undeserving of normal human connection.

Think of it like this: imagine a school cafeteria. One day, an entire friend group decides to stop talking to one student — they don't save them a seat, they don't reply to their messages, they walk past them without acknowledgment. That student hasn't gone anywhere, but socially, they've been pushed outside the group's invisible walls. That is ostracism.

"Ostracize" is not a gentle word. It carries real weight. Here's what makes it distinct from simpler words like "exclude" or "ignore":

It is deliberate. Ostracizing is never an accident. It's a purposeful act — the group chooses to shut someone out.

It is collective. Usually, it's not just one person turning their back. It's a group, a community, a society, or an institution doing it together. This is what makes it so powerful and painful — the person faces rejection from multiple sides at once.

It is sustained. It's not a brief cold shoulder. Ostracism tends to be ongoing, not a one-time snub.

It targets belonging. Humans have a deep need to belong. Ostracism attacks that need directly, which is why being ostracized is one of the most emotionally painful experiences a person can have. Studies in psychology consistently show that social exclusion activates the same parts of the brain as physical pain.
The Range of Situations Where It's Used

"Ostracize" works across many different scales and settings:

Social / Personal: A teenager who breaks an unspoken rule of their friend group and gets completely shut out by all their peers is being ostracized.

Professional / Workplace: A whistleblower who exposes wrongdoing in their company might find that all their colleagues suddenly stop talking to them, exclude them from meetings, and treat them like a pariah. They have been ostracized by their professional community.

Community / Cultural: Someone who goes against the deeply held beliefs of their town, religion, or cultural community might find themselves shunned by everyone they grew up with — uninvited to gatherings, spoken about in hushed disapproval, no longer considered "one of us."

Political / National: Countries can ostracize other countries too — cutting off diplomatic ties, refusing to cooperate, isolating them on the world stage. A nation that violates international norms might find itself ostracized by the global community.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

When you use "ostracize," you are signaling that something serious has happened. It is not a neutral or mild word. It implies:

  • A judgment was made against the person.
  • The group acted with intention.
  • The excluded person likely feels humiliated, lonely, and powerless.
  • The exclusion carries a kind of social punishment — the group is sending a message.

This is important because it means you wouldn't use "ostracize" to describe small, everyday social slights. If a friend forgets to invite you to one dinner, that's not ostracism. But if your entire social circle freezes you out, stops acknowledging your existence, and treats you as a social outcast over a prolonged period — that is ostracism.
How to Use It in a Sentence

Here are examples that show the word doing real work:

  • "After he reported the corruption, his colleagues ostracized him completely — no one would even eat lunch with him."
  • "She was ostracized by her community for marrying outside her religion."
  • "The other children ostracized the new kid for weeks before one kind classmate finally reached out."
  • "The country was ostracized by its neighbors following the invasion."
  • "He feared that speaking his true opinion would get him ostracized from the group."

Notice that the word is often followed by "by" (ostracized by the group) or "from" (ostracized from the community).
How It Differs From Similar Words

Exclude — broader and more neutral. You can exclude someone from a list, a meeting, or a competition for perfectly neutral reasons. "Ostracize" always implies deliberate social rejection with a punishing quality.

Shun — very similar to ostracize, but "shun" often feels more personal and individual. One person can shun another. "Ostracize" more strongly implies a group pushing someone out.

Ignore — much milder. Ignoring someone might be accidental or temporary. Ostracizing is deliberate and sustained.

Banish / Exile — these usually involve physically removing someone from a place. Ostracism is social — the person remains in the same space, but is treated as an outcast within it. That's actually what makes it more insidious.

Blacklist — to blacklist someone is to officially bar them from something (a job, an industry, an opportunity). Ostracism is broader and more social, not necessarily linked to a formal list or institution.
One Final Way to Think About It

Imagine a circle of people. To ostracize someone is to draw that circle deliberately around a group — and make sure one specific person is left outside of it, with everyone inside knowing exactly what they're doing and why.

It is rejection made into a group project. And that is precisely why the word carries so much weight.
11497:
Otiose means serving no useful purpose — something that is there, but contributes nothing. It is pointless, unnecessary, redundant, or ineffective.

Think of it this way: if you added something to a situation and removing it would change absolutely nothing, that thing is otiose. It takes up space — in a sentence, in a plan, in an argument, in a process — without earning its place.

In language and writing, a word or phrase is otiose when it adds no new meaning:

"She is a young girl who is female and youthful."

The words female and youthful are otiose here — young girl already told us everything. They are not wrong, just completely unnecessary.

In arguments and discussions, a point is otiose when it is futile to make — either because it changes nothing, proves nothing, or because the matter is already settled:

"After the contract was signed, his objections were otiose."

His objections didn't matter anymore. Raising them served no purpose.

In actions and efforts, something is otiose when it is ineffective or pointless in practice:

"All their elaborate precautions proved otiose when the storm bypassed the town entirely."

The precautions did nothing — not because they were badly designed, but because the situation made them irrelevant.

There is a second, rarer meaning of otiose: idle or at leisure — describing a person who is doing nothing, resting, or being lazy. You might still encounter this in older literature:

"He spent his afternoons in an otiose haze, watching clouds from his window."

This meaning is now quite rare in modern English. If you see otiose in a contemporary book, article, or essay, it almost certainly carries the first meaning — serving no useful purpose.
The Precise Flavour of the Word

This is the key to truly understanding otiose — it's not just a fancy word for "useless." It has a specific flavour:

Something useless might have never had a purpose — a broken tool, a dead battery.

Something otiose tends to be unnecessary in this particular context — it might be fine elsewhere, but here it adds nothing. A long disclaimer at the end of a private note between close friends isn't useless in the abstract, but it is otiose there. A safety warning on a product used only by experts isn't evil — it's just otiose.

So otiose often implies redundancy or superfluousness rather than absolute worthlessness. It is the excess that could be cut without loss.

This is why writers, lawyers, philosophers, and academics love this word. It is perfect for pointing out that something — a clause, a step, a distinction, an argument — is technically present but functionally hollow.
Who Uses This Word and Where

Otiose is a formal, literary word. You will encounter it in:

  • Academic writing and philosophy
  • Legal writing
  • Literary criticism and essays
  • Sophisticated journalism
  • Older novels

You would almost never hear it in everyday conversation. If someone used it casually at a dinner table, it would sound deliberately elevated or even showy. In writing, however, it is precise and perfectly appropriate.

• It does not mean overly complicated (that would be convoluted or labyrinthine).
  • It does not mean incorrect or wrong — something otiose can be perfectly correct, just unnecessary.
  • It does not mean harmful — otiose things are inert, not damaging.
  • It does not necessarily mean boring, though otiose writing often becomes tedious as a consequence.

Whenever you see or hear otiose, ask: "Is this earning its place? Does it change anything? Would removing it cost us anything?"

If the answer is no — it's otiose.
11498: The word "ottoman" has two distinct meanings as a noun — one refers to a piece of furniture, and the other refers to a type of fabric. The furniture meaning is by far the more common one in everyday life, so we'll cover that first and in the most depth.

An ottoman is a low, cushioned, upholstered piece of furniture that has no back and no arms. That last part is what sets it apart from almost every other piece of furniture you can think of. A sofa has a back and arms. An armchair has a back and arms. A bench has a back (usually). An ottoman has neither — it's essentially a firm, soft-topped block that you can sit on, rest your feet on, or use in other ways.

It sits close to the floor, is always padded and covered in fabric, leather, or similar material, and comes in many shapes — square, rectangular, round, or even hexagonal.

What is it used for?

An ottoman is a remarkably versatile piece of furniture. Here are its main uses:

1. As a footrest
This is its most classic use. You sit in a sofa or armchair, and you place your feet up on the ottoman in front of you. It's meant for comfort and relaxation — the same way you'd stretch your legs out on a coffee table, but softer and more comfortable.

2. As extra seating
Because the top surface is cushioned, people can sit on an ottoman just like they'd sit on a stool. When you have extra guests and not enough chairs, an ottoman steps in as a seat.

3. As a coffee table
A larger, flatter ottoman placed at the center of a living room can function as a coffee table — you place a tray on top with drinks, books, or snacks. Because it's softer than a table, it's also safer if you have young children running around.

4. As a decorative accent
Even if no one is actively using it, an ottoman adds warmth, color, and texture to a room. Interior designers often use ottomans to make a living space feel more inviting and complete.

Storage Ottomans

One of the most popular modern variants is the storage ottoman. It looks like a regular ottoman from the outside, but the top is actually a lid that lifts open, revealing a hollow compartment inside. People use this hidden space to store blankets, pillows, remote controls, toys, magazines — anything you want tucked away but within easy reach. It is furniture that doubles as a storage solution, which makes it especially popular in smaller homes and apartments.

Common Types and Styles

While they all share the same basic idea, ottomans come in several recognizable forms:

  • Footstool ottoman — Small and simple, placed directly in front of a chair or sofa, purely for resting your feet.
  • Cocktail ottoman (also called a coffee table ottoman) — Larger and typically rectangular. Sits at the center of a seating area and serves the dual role of footrest and coffee table surface.
  • Cube ottoman — Perfectly square in shape, compact and versatile. Can be used as a seat, a footrest, or a side table.
  • Bench ottoman — Long and narrow, like a bench. Often placed at the foot of a bed or along a wall.
  • Tufted ottoman — Has buttons sewn into the fabric in a grid pattern, pulling the material inward to create a classic, decorative dimpled look.
  • Round ottoman — Circular in shape, often used as a central accent piece in a room.

Where you'll typically find an ottoman

  • In a living room, in front of a sofa or armchair
  • At the foot of a bed in a bedroom (usually a bench-style ottoman)
  • In a home office, as a companion to a reading chair
  • In hotel lobbies and lounges, where they serve as casual seating

Less commonly, ottoman also refers to a type of woven fabric characterized by prominent horizontal ridges or ribs running across its width. These ribs are raised and visible, giving the fabric a distinctly textured, almost ribbed appearance — similar in feel to corduroy, but the ridges run horizontally rather than vertically, and the fabric has a slightly silkier or stiffer quality depending on the material.

Ottoman fabric is made from silk, cotton, wool, or blends of these, and has historically been used in:

  • Formal clothing such as jackets, coats, and dresses
  • Upholstery for furniture (including, fittingly, the cushioned seats of ottomans)
  • Accessories like ribbons and trims

When someone in fashion or textiles says "ottoman," they mean this ribbed fabric — not the furniture.

What it isKey feature

Think of an ottoman as the most relaxed, easygoing piece of furniture in a room. It has no pretensions — no tall back, no fancy arms. To oust someone means to forcefully push them out of a position of power, authority, or control — usually against their will.

When someone is ousted, they don't leave on their own. They are made to leave, often by people who have the power or numbers to do so.

Think of it this way: imagine a king sitting on a throne. He didn't choose to leave. He was pushed off that throne by someone stronger, or by a group that turned against him. That's ousting.

The word almost always involves three things:

  1. A person in a position (a leader, a boss, a ruler, an official)
  2. Someone being removed from that position
  3. The removal happening by force, pressure, or authority — not by the person's own free choice

This is where it gets interesting. English has many words for removing people — fire, dismiss, expel, remove, overthrow. "Oust" is not exactly the same as any of them. Here's what makes it unique:

It always implies a struggle or a contest for power. The person being ousted usually wanted to stay. They had some level of power or standing, and someone else took it away from them. There is always a sense of conflict underneath the word.

  • A company fires an employee → routine employment action, top-down
  • A school expels a student → disciplinary action, institutional
  • A crowd overthrows a dictator → violent, revolutionary
  • Someone ousts a leader → removes them from their seat of power, often through political maneuvering, votes, pressure, or force

"Oust" sits in the space between "remove" (too neutral) and "overthrow" (too violent). It implies deliberate, purposeful removal — with some level of effort or power behind it — but doesn't necessarily mean physical violence.

Very importantly, you oust someone who has power or authority. You wouldn't say "the teacher ousted the student from the classroom." You'd say the teacher expelled or removed the student.

But you would say:

  • "The army ousted the president." (president = position of power)
  • "The board ousted the CEO." (CEO = position of authority)
  • "Protesters ousted the corrupt governor." (governor = official power)

The word is most natural when the person being removed is in charge of something — a country, a company, an organization, or a territory.

You will most commonly see "oust" in:

Politics — governments, elections, coups, and power struggles
→ "The military ousted the elected leader in a sudden coup."

Business — boardrooms, shareholder disputes, corporate takeovers
→ "Investors ousted the chairman after years of poor performance."

History — describing the fall of rulers, dynasties, or regimes
→ "The revolution ousted the monarchy after centuries of rule."

Sports management — coaches and managers being forced out
→ "The club ousted its manager after a string of defeats."

"Oust" is a strong, dramatic word. When a writer or journalist chooses "oust" instead of "remove" or "replace," they are telling you something: this was not peaceful, this was not agreed upon, and the person who left did not want to go. It signals conflict, power, and consequence.

It is also a fairly formal word. You would normally read it in newspapers, political reporting, or books — not in casual everyday conversation. In everyday speech, people might say "they kicked him out" or "they got rid of her" instead. But "oust" carries more weight and precision.

Oust = to remove someone from a position of power or authority, against their will, using force, political pressure, or collective action.

The person ousted had power. They didn't choose to leave. Someone made them go.
